newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council, officials chastise Kabila on refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council, officials chastise Kabila on refugees.

text.p: Security Council members on Thursday expressed "grave concern" at killing of refugees in eastern Zaire and attacks on U.N. staff, particularly the recent assault against two staff members by rebel soldiers.

Council President Park Soo Gil of South Korea said council members shared a "sense of aversion" about the attacks on humanitarian workers in general and the U.N. Children's Fund or UNICEF in particular in rebel territory.

Two UNICEF staff on Monday were assaulted and physically beaten in Goma, close to rebel leader Laurent Kabila's headquarters. The attackers were in uniform. U.N. sources said they spoke Kinyarwandan, the language of neighbouring Rwanda whose rulers are backing the Tutsi-dominated rebels in Zaire.

U.N. officials on Wednesday called together senior diplomats close to the Zaire crisis to use their influence with Kabila and such allies as Rwanda in connection with the refugees and the UNICEF attack.
Kabila was notified directly by a senior U.N. official of the attack, which was said to be more brutal than initial reports indicated, U.N. sources said.

Carol Bellamy, executive director of UNICEF, on Thursday again expressed outrage and called the attack "absolutely horrific," saying the aid workers were there "to try to provide minimal type of assistance to children who are barely alive."

Park said Security Council members also were "seriously concerned" over reports of killings of Rwandan refugees by the rebels as well as the "obstruction" by Kabila's forces to allow a U.N. probe into the massacres.
U.N. investigators and forensic experts on May 9 planned to dig up mass graves in a mission seen as a litmus test for Kabila's willingness to assist human rights investigations.

More than half a million Rwandan Hutus went home in late 1996 but UNHCR says up to 300,000 remain in Zaire. Rwanda says only 50,000 Hutu refugees are left, a figure once accepted by the United States and Britain in calling off a multinational protection force for the refugees.

The refugees are among the remnants of the Hutus who fled into Zaire from Rwanda in fear of reprisal for the 1994 Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis. The United Nations argues that many are innocent women and children who were caught in two countries' civil wars.
